description: I am a university student for C.U.T representing the new technologies group
summary:
Our project is an “Earth Information Jukebox” that turns NASA Earth imagery into accessible sound. We developed a browser-based tool, plus a Python command-line version, that maps colors in satellite maps to data values, sweeps across the image in stereo, and plays time-based sonifications so users can hear how Earth is changing. It includes spoken summaries, keyboard controls, and “only what changed” mode to highlight increases and decreases across regions.
This addresses the NASA challenge by making Earth observation data more accessible to blind and low-vision users, especially where most environmental information is currently visual-only. It matters because climate and environmental change are urgent global issues, and inclusive tools help more people understand, monitor, and respond to them. By combining scientific data with music and narration, the project makes complex planetary trends easier to experience and interpret.
details:
What it does and how it works

Earth Jukebox turns NASA Earth-observation maps into sound, so people can study them without seeing them. The web app takes a map image, such as night lights from "Black Marble", NO₂ or sea surface temperature, and reads the colours back into data values using the map’s colorbar. It then plays a sweep across the map: pitch shows north to south, left-to-right position follows the map west to east, and loudness shows how high the value is. It also gives a spoken and written description of the map, covering the regions with the most data and the average.

Users can listen to one frame, or to what changed between two frames, such as which regions got brighter or dimmer. In Explore mode they point at a place on the map and hear only that spot. They can load their own map images, adjust speed and volume, and download the sound as a WAV file. Everything works from the keyboard, and a guided tour introduces the features.

Benefits

  • Blind and low-vision people can get information that is normally only available as colours and shapes.
  • Sighted people can use it as a second way to notice patterns and changes.
  • It runs in a browser with nothing to install, and users can bring their own maps.

Intended impact

We want Earth data to be accessible to everyone. A blind student or researcher should be able to ask the same questions of a NASA map as a sighted one, such as where it is brightest and what changed over time. [One line from your tester about what they heard or learned.]

Tools and technologies

  • Web app: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, using the Web Audio API for sound, the canvas for drawing, and the browser’s speech synthesis for spoken descriptions.
  • Python prototype: OpenCV and NumPy, with YOLOv8n (ultralytics) in the first experiments. The final app doesn’t use YOLO, because it detects objects rather than reading data maps.
  • Testing: an automated check suite in Node.
  • Hardware: none special, only a browser on a computer or phone.

What is creative about it

Most tools turn maps into sound from raw data files. Ours works from the map images people already have, and recovers the values using the colorbar. That means any map with a colorbar can be used. The Change mode, Explore cursor and spoken descriptions let someone question the map instead of only listening to it.

Factors we considered

  • Accessibility first: full keyboard use, shortcuts, screen-reader support, and voice that can be switched off.
  • Accuracy: a map is only decoded where its colours match the colorbar, and we say so when too little matches. We also tell users that this is an image-based approximation, not the original data.
  • Comfort: the sound is smooth and not harsh, with speed and volume controls.
  • Honesty: we’re clear about the limits and credit the NASA datasets.
